source_text: Nam in illo opere, quod te supra dixi nuper Romam misisse, audacius quid sentires aperuisti. In primo enim libro, cum tibi similiter proposuisses quod nos obicimus, arbitrium vos liberum denegare, ita disseris constantissimus et subtilissimus disputator. Quis autem nostrum dicat, quod primi hominis peccato perierit liberum arbitrium de genere humano? Libertas quidem periit per peccatum, sed illa quae in paradiso fuit, habendi plenam cum immortalitate iustitiam; propter quod natura humana divina indiget gratia, dicente Domino in Evangelio suo: " vos Filius liberaverit, tunc vere liberi eritis " [n230] , utique liberi ad bene iusteque vivendum. Nam liberum arbitrium usque adeo in peccatore non periit, ut per ipsum peccent, maxime omnes qui cum delectatione peccant et amore peccati, et eis placet quod eos libet. Unde Apostolus: "m essetis - inquit <197> servi peccati, liberi fuistis iustitiae " [n231] . Ecce ostenduntur etiam peccato minime potuisse, nisi alia libertate, servire. Liberi ergo a iustitia non sunt, nisi arbitrio libertatis; liberi autem a peccato non fiunt, nisi gratia Salvatoris. Propter quod admirabilis Doctor etiam verba ipsa discrevit: "m enim servi essetis - inquit <197> peccati, liberi fuistis iustitiae. Quem ergo tunc fructum habuistis in his, in quibus nunc erubescitis? Nam finis illorum mors est; nunc autem liberati a peccato, servi autem facti Dei, habetis fructum vestrum in sanctificationem, finem vero vitam aeternam " [n232] . Liberos dixit iustitiae, non liberatos; a peccato autem non liberos, ne sibi hoc tribuerent, sed vigilantissime maluit dicere liberatos; referens hoc ad illam Domini sententiam: " vos Filius liberaverit, tunc vere liberi eritis ". Cum itaque non vivant bene filii hominum, nisi effecti filii Dei, quid est quod iste libero arbitrio vult bene vivendi tribuere potestatem; cum enim haec potestas non detur nisi "atia Dei, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum " [n233] , dicente Evangelio: "Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri " [n234] . Et item post modicum: Datur ergo, inquis, potestas ut filii Dei fiant, qui credunt in eum. Quae potestas, nisi detur a Deo, nulla esse potest ex libero arbitrio; quia nec liberum in bono erit, quod liberator non liberaverit; sed in malum liberum habet arbitrium, cui delectationem malitiae vel occultus vel manifestus deceptor insevit, vel sibi ipse persuasit. Non itaque, sicut dicunt nos quidam dicere, et iste audet insuper scribere, omnes in peccatum, velut inviti, carnis suae necessitate coguntur; sed si iam in ea aetate sunt, ut propriae mentis utantur arbitrio, et in peccato sua voluntate retinentur, et a peccato in peccatum sua voluntate praecipitantur. Sed haec voluntas, quae libera est in malis, quia delectatur malis, ideo libera in bonis non est, quia liberata non est. Nec potest homo boni aliquid velle, nisi adiuvetur ab eo qui malum non potest velle [n235] . In his omnibus verbis tuis, quae posui, ita video gratiae nomen cum liberi arbitrii negatione consertum, ut non tam mala sensus tui appellationum bonis vindicari queant, quam dignitas nominum dogmatum tuorum adhaesione vilescat. Non ergo te his sermonibus honestasti, sed ornamenta ipsa turpasti. Nos tamen ea quae a te iuncta sunt, separamus, ut gratiae divinitas ab scaevis colligationibus enodata, nec responsione quatiatur; et gravitate Catholicorum, non Manichaeorum adulatione laudetur. Gratiam ergo Christi multiplicem confitemur. Primum munus eius est, quod facti ex nihilo sumus. Secundum, quod ut viventibus sensu, ita sentientibus ratione praestamus; quae impressa est animo, ut Conditoris imago doceretur: ad cuius aeque respicit dignitatem arbitrii concessa libertas. Ipsi etiam gratiae beneficiorum quae nobis praestare non desinit, augmenta reputamus. Ipsa gratia legem in adiutorium misit [n236] ; ad eius spectabat officium, ut rationis lumen, quod pravitatis exempla hebetabant et consuetudo vitiorum, multimodis eruditionibus excitaret, atque invitatu suo foveret. Ad istius ergo gratiae, id est, divinae benevolentiae, quae rebus causam dedit, plenitudinem spectavit, ut Verbum caro fieret, et habitaret in nobis [n237] . Reposcens enim Deus ab imagine sua amoris vicem, palam fecit quam totum in nos inaestimabili egisset affectu, ut vel sero redamaremus eum, qui commendans caritatem suam nobis [n238] , Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis illum tradidit [n239] ; pollicens quia si voluissemus deinceps voluntati eius oboedire, Unigeniti sui praestaret nos esse cohaeredes [n240] .
pass_a_gloss: For in that work, which I said above you recently sent to Rome, you opened more audaciously what you were sensing. For in the first book, when you had similarly set before yourself what we object, that you deny free choice, you discuss thus, most constant and most subtle disputant. But who of us says, that by the sin of the first human free choice perished from the human race? Liberty indeed perished through sin, but that which was in paradise, of having full justice with immortality; on account of which human nature needs divine grace, the Lord saying in his Gospel: If the Son shall have freed you, then you will be truly free, that is free toward living well and justly. For free choice has so far not perished in the sinner, that through it they sin, especially all who sin with delight and with love of sin, and that which pleases them pleases them. Whence the Apostle: When you were slaves of sin, you were free of justice. See they are shown to have been able least even to serve sin, except by another liberty. They are therefore free from justice only by the choice of liberty; but they do not become free from sin, except by the grace of the Savior. On account of which the admirable Teacher also distinguished the words themselves: For when you were slaves of sin, you were free of justice. What fruit therefore did you then have in these, in which now you blush? For the end of those is death; but now having been freed from sin, but made slaves of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, but the end eternal life. He said free of justice, not freed; but from sin not free, lest they attribute this to themselves, but most vigilantly he preferred to say freed; referring this to that sentence of the Lord: If the Son shall have freed you, then you will be truly free. When therefore the sons of humans do not live well, unless made sons of God, what is it that this man wants to attribute to free choice the power of living well; when indeed this power is not given except by the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, the Gospel saying: But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God. And likewise after a little: Power is therefore given, you say, that they may become sons of God, who believe in him. Which power, unless it be given by God, can be none from free choice; because neither will it be free in the good, which the liberator shall not have freed; but into evil he has free choice, into whom a hidden or open deceiver has sown a delight of malice, or he himself persuaded himself. Not therefore, as certain say we say, and this man dares besides to write, are all forced into sin, as if unwilling, by the necessity of their flesh; but if they are already in that age, that they use the choice of their own mind, both they are retained in sin by their own will, and from sin into sin they are thrown headlong by their own will. But this will, which is free in evils, because it is delighted by evils, therefore is not free in goods, because it has not been freed. Nor can a human will anything of good, unless he is helped by him who cannot will evil. In all these words of yours, which I placed, I so see the name of grace sewn together with a denial of free choice, that not so much can the evils of your sense be vindicated by the goods of namings, as the dignity of the names cheapens by adhesion of your dogmas. You have not therefore made yourself honorable by these speeches, but you have fouled the ornaments themselves. We nevertheless separate those things which have been joined by you, that the divinity of grace, unknotted from left-handed colligations, may neither be shaken by an answer; and may be praised by the gravity of Catholics, not by the flattery of Manichaeans. We confess therefore the multiple grace of Christ. Its first gift is, that we have been made from nothing. The second, that as we excel the living by sense, so we excel those sensing by reason; which has been impressed on the mind, that the image of the Founder may be taught: to whose dignity equally the conceded liberty of choice looks. To that same grace we also reckon the increases of benefits which it does not cease to furnish to us. That grace itself sent the law into help; it was looking to its office, that it would stir by many-modeled eruditions the light of reason, which examples of crookedness and the custom of vices were dulling, and would foster it by its own invitation. To the fullness therefore of this grace, that is, of divine benevolence, which gave a cause to things, it looked, that the Word would become flesh, and would dwell in us. For God, claiming back from his image a turn of love, made open how he had driven the whole in us with inestimable affection, that even late we might love him back, who commending his love to us, did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us; promising that if we had been willing thereafter to obey his will, he would furnish us to be coheirs of his Only-begotten.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: In the work which I said above you recently sent to Rome, you revealed your meaning more boldly. In its first book, having similarly set before yourself our charge that you deny free choice, you argue as follows, you most consistent and subtle debater: “Which of us says that through the first human being's sin free choice perished from the human race? Freedom indeed perished through sin, but the freedom that existed in paradise to possess complete righteousness with immortality. Human nature therefore needs divine grace, as the Lord says in his Gospel: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free’ (John 8:36), that is, free to live well and justly. Free choice has so far not perished in the sinner that through it people sin, especially all who sin with pleasure and love of sin and approve what they enjoy. Hence the apostle says: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness’ (Romans 6:20). See, they are shown to have been unable even to serve sin except by another sort of freedom. They are free from righteousness only by freedom of choice, but are freed from sin only by the Savior's grace. For this reason that admirable teacher carefully distinguished even the words: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you then have in the things of which you are now ashamed? Their end is death. But now, freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification and your end eternal life’ (Romans 6:20–22). He called them free from righteousness, not freed from it. But regarding sin he very carefully preferred to call them not free, lest they attribute this to themselves, but freed, referring this to the Lord's statement: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free.’ Since the children of humanity do not live well unless they become God's children, why does this man want to attribute the power of living well to free choice? This power is given only by ‘God's grace through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 7:25), as the Gospel says: ‘To as many as received him he gave power to become God's children’” (John 1:12; Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.2.4).

A little later you say again: “The power is therefore given to those who believe in him to become God's children. Unless God gives this power, none can come from free choice. For what the liberator has not freed will not be free for good. But a person has choice free for evil when a hidden or open deceiver has implanted delight in wickedness, or when that person has persuaded himself to it. Thus it is not the case, as some say we claim and as this man even dares to write, that everyone is forced into sin against his will, as it were, by the necessity of his flesh. Rather, if people are old enough to exercise the choice of their own mind, they are held in sin by their own will and plunge from sin into sin by their own will. But this will, free in evil because it delights in evil, is not free in good because it has not been freed. A human being cannot will anything good unless helped by the one who cannot will evil” (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.6–7).

In all these words of yours that I have quoted, I see grace's name so entangled with denial of free choice that the goodness of the names cannot vindicate the evil of your meaning. Rather, the dignity of the names is degraded by attachment to your doctrines. You have not made yourself honorable by these words; you have dishonored the ornaments themselves. We, however, separate what you have joined, so that the divinity of grace, disentangled from these perverse connections, will suffer no attack from our reply and will be praised with catholic seriousness rather than Manichaean flattery.

We therefore acknowledge Christ's grace in its many forms. Its first gift is that we were made from nothing. Its second is that, just as through sensation we surpass things that merely live, so through reason we surpass things that sense. Reason was impressed upon the mind to disclose the Creator's image; the granted freedom of choice belongs equally to that dignity (compare Genesis 1:26–27). To this same grace we credit the increase of benefits he never ceases to bestow on us. This grace sent the Law as a help (Isaiah 8:20, LXX wording). Its task was to awaken by many kinds of teaching, and nourish by its invitation, the light of reason that examples of wrongdoing and habitual vices were dimming. To the fullness of this grace, that is, the divine goodwill that gave things their existence, belonged the Word's becoming flesh and dwelling among us (John 1:14). For God, asking his image to return his love, made clear with what immeasurable affection he had done everything for us. Thus we might, even if late, love in return the one who, commending his love toward us (Romans 5:8), did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us (Romans 8:32), promising that if we henceforth chose to obey his will, he would make us fellow heirs with his Only Begotten (Romans 8:17).

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. variants.reading: “The Law as a help” follows the source’s reference to the LXX form of Isaiah 8:20, whose wording differs from familiar modern translations. Augustine’s argument about “free” and “freed” is retained because the distinction itself is being contested.
